extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, judges, agency lawyers, and policymakers interested in First Amendment limits on federal agency use of social media
extracted.subtask_short: agency social media First Amendment analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and doctrinal tests for whether speech on or selected by federal agency social media platforms is government speech or private speech subject to the public forum doctrine. Focuses on contextual factors, agency intent, control, site ownership, and institutional role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government-speech prong — government has established a message
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Johanns test, the first prong is to find that the government has established a message; courts look for a clear governmental message (as in Page) but may accept more obscure or institutional "editorial discretion" or "connoisseurship" (as in Gittens) as sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency mission statements and explicit declarations of purpose for social media (e.g., EPA: further its mission; State Dept.: engage audiences on issues relevant to U.S. foreign policy) are relevant evidence. A clear message is not strictly required; selection aiming to convey a particular tone (e.g., "civilized engagement") may be advanced but may stretch government-speech doctrine toward absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government-speech prong — effective control over content and dissemination
rubrics_metrics.description: The second Johanns prong requires the government to exercise effective control over the content and dissemination of the message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence of moderation practices (especially pre-screening), consistent screening before posting, or substantial editorial control supports finding effective control. Few agencies pre-screen; meeting the control bar requires agency manpower/resources. Even inconsistent control can suffice (Downs v. LAUSD).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional-role/institution-specific analysis (government enterprise cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the government is acting in an institutional role (patron of the arts, broadcaster, librarian, university, etc.) for which selectivity is inherent—if so, selection of private speech may be treated as government speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Finley, Forbes, and American Library A. show that when government acts as patron or institutional operator, viewpoint discrimination may be inherent in functioning (e.g., National Gallery choosing which paintings to hang). Courts perform a contextual, institutionally specific inquiry to determine if this applies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and purposive analysis (no categorical rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Which doctrine applies depends on context, purpose, and pragmatism; courts avoid blanket rules and instead scrutinize the precise nature of the government's role and the circumstances of the forum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One cannot simply transplant government-speech doctrine onto social media because selection/editorial discretion exists; instead, judges should analyze whether the agency is providing a forum for discourse or speaking itself. The analysis is "context driven and pragmatic."

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-forum test — intent to open forum
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Perry, a public forum is identified by government intent: the government must take affirmative steps to open a forum for private speech; statements of intent and evidence of practice/tacit approval are relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts often view intent narrowly and may permit the government to define the forum or subject matter very specifically. Presidential memoranda and agency social-media statements encouraging participation are strong evidence of intent to open a forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-forum test — historical use and compatibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Perry also looks to historical use of the forum and whether the use is compatible with the forum's purpose (e.g., parks as places for speeches and other transitory expressive acts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical practices and whether the property or medium can accommodate a large number of speakers affect the analysis. The permanence/transitory distinction (monuments vs oratory) is relevant—permanent installations may be more susceptible to government-speech reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predominance test — whether government or private speech predominates
rubrics_metrics.description: Because both government and private speech can appear on agency social-media sites, courts should assess which type predominates to decide whether government-speech or public-forum doctrine applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to weigh include explicit agency messages, degree of editorial control or moderation, site ownership (.gov vs private platform), and how the site is characterized ("agency sponsored").

rubrics_metrics.name: Site ownership and private-platform complication
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the social-media venue is public property (.gov/agency blog) or private property (Facebook, Twitter) complicates public-forum analysis: private property used for public purpose does not automatically preclude a public-forum finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agency use of a private platform is analogous to leasing space for a town meeting; designation as "agency sponsored" and the extent of government operation/administration are relevant to determining a forum's status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easement analogy — comments as easement akin to public forum
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting the public to comment on agency-sponsored sites is akin to providing speakers with an easement to use public property; when an easement exists, public-forum principles are implicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the circumstances resemble a classic public forum (an easement), the agency should be treated as having opened a forum for private speech rather than engaging in government speech by selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanence vs. transitory distinction (monuments vs. oratory)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court has distinguished permanent monuments (where government speech may permit viewpoint discrimination) from transitory expressive acts (speeches, marches), which favor public-forum analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because social-media comments are ephemeral (evanescent) rather than permanent, the analogy to monuments is weak and supports applying public-forum protections rather than government-speech deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation practices as evidence of control (pre-screening vs post-moderation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an agency screens comments before posting (pre-screening) or merely removes some comments after posting (post-moderation) is material to whether the agency exercises effective control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-screening is the highest level of control and strongly supports government-speech characterization; post-moderation suggests less control. Resource constraints make pre-screening uncommon among agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency statements of purpose and labeling as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: How an agency describes its social-media presence (e.g., "U.S. Dept. of State on Facebook," "using social media to further our mission," "we encourage you to share your thoughts") is probative of intent and of the government's attempt to define the forum or message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling a page as the agency's presence on a private platform may be an attempt to cast the site as a government enterprise; courts will consider such statements along with actual practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between formalized comment processes and informal social media
rubrics_metrics.description: Formal administrative comment processes (e.g., Regulations.gov) are structured and distinct from informal social-media comment spaces; social-media sites opened for transparency/participation do not present characteristics of a formalized structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because social media lacks the formal characteristics of rulemaking comment processes or town meetings, the public-forum doctrine is argued to be more appropriate for protecting citizen comments on agency social media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of viewpoint discrimination and abuse absent clear policy
rubrics_metrics.description: When a government website or social-media page lacks a formal policy articulating what private speech is permitted, findings of government speech based on selection/approval risk permitting impermissible viewpoint discrimination or obscuring whether rejections are message-driven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts are wary that treating selection alone as government speech could allow agencies to engage in viewpoint discrimination; the absence of explicit policies increases this risk (Torruella concurrence in Page/Gittens noted).
